title: The Multitasking Myth
objective: After this level you can explain why switching between tasks costs time and accuracy.
summary: Multitasking is mostly rapid switching, and each switch makes you slower and more error-prone. Phone conversations, even hands-free, pull attention from the road.

cards.headline: Doing two things at once? You're probably switching.
cards.body: Some researchers suggest that unless a task is fully automatic, multitasking is really your attention flicking back and forth between tasks. Switching sounds free. It isn't.

cards.headline: The switch cost
cards.body: In task-switching experiments, people alternate between simple tasks. Right after each switch, they respond substantially slower and usually make more errors. Psychologists call this the switch cost. A moment to prepare shrinks it, but doesn't make it disappear. In a 2001 study by Rubinstein and colleagues, the time lost grew as the rules of the tasks got more complex.

cards.headline: It's the conversation, not your hands
cards.body: In a 2001 driving-simulator study, phone conversations doubled the rate of missed traffic signals and slowed reactions to the ones drivers caught. Hands-free phones were no better than handheld ones. Listening to the radio or a book on tape didn't hurt at all. Later eye-tracking studies found that drivers on the phone were less likely to recognize things they had looked at, a form of inattentional blindness.

cards.fact: In a 2010 study of 200 people, 2.5 percent, about 1 in 40, showed no cost at all.
cards.context: Researchers called them supertaskers: they drove in a simulator while doing a demanding memory and math task with no drop in performance. For everyone else, combining the tasks made performance worse.

cards.headline: Multitasking, examined
learned: Each switch costs time and accuracy
Phone calls impair driving, hands-free too
Only about 1 in 40 showed no cost

questions.prompt: In task-switching experiments, what happens to responses right after people switch tasks?

options.label: They get faster, since the brain is warmed up
options.rationale: Responses slow down after a switch.

options.label: They are slower and usually less accurate
They are unchanged if people practice
options.rationale: Preparation shrinks the cost but doesn't remove it.

options.label: They stop until the new rules are memorized
options.rationale: People keep responding, just more slowly.

questions.explanation: Right after a switch, responses are substantially slower and usually more error-prone: the switch cost.

questions.prompt: Why did hands-free phone calls impair simulated driving about as much as handheld ones?

options.label: Hands-free devices are harder to operate while steering
Drivers hold the wheel less tightly on calls
Any sound in the car distracts drivers
options.rationale: The radio and a book on tape didn't hurt driving.

options.label: The talking itself draws attention away

questions.explanation: Radio and recorded books didn't impair driving, but conversations did, hands-free or not: the cost comes from attention, not hands.

questions.prompt: Drivers on the phone often failed to recognize things they had looked at, the Level 17 idea of _____.

options.label: sensory adaptation
options.rationale: That comes from a stimulus staying constant.

options.label: the McGurk effect
options.rationale: That's sight changing what you hear.

options.label: Weber's law
options.rationale: That's about noticing changes in intensity.

questions.explanation: With attention on the conversation, drivers missed what was in plain view: inattentional blindness, as in the gorilla study.
